title: Information-driven stepping in dimeric transport motors
authors: Antonio Patrón Castro, David A. Sivak
abstract: Dimeric transport motors are nanoscale protein complexes that move along cytoskeletal filaments. Here we introduce a theoretical model for their stepping dynamics, in which the two motor heads undergo Brownian motion with mobilities periodically switching in a position-dependent manner so that only one head moves at a time. Through consumption of chemical free energy, this mechanism produces directed motion. We characterize at steady state the motor's mean velocity and its energy and information flows. The motor operates as a pure information engine, where only information is transduced between its components, without energy exchange. For localized switching, the model yields a thermodynamically consistent expression for the mean motor velocity that reproduces experimentally observed behavior, and captures the stall force characteristic of tightly coupled motors. Finally, coarse-graining the model to a single mechanical degree of freedom produces a second-order non-Markovian dynamics, from which we compute the four distinct dwell-time distributions that can be directly observed in single-molecule experiments. Our findings highlight how information transduction, via implicit operation as a Maxwell demon, may underlie the remarkable performance of these molecular motors.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical model for dimeric molecular motors that move by coupling Brownian motion with chemically controlled mobility switching. It argues that the motor functions as an information engine, generating directed motion solely through information processing rather than net energy flow. The key output is the prediction of measurable dwell-time distributions derived from this non-Markovian dynamics.
main_problem: The study aims to theoretically model how dimeric transport motors achieve directed motion by operating as a 'pure information engine,' suggesting that information transduction, rather than net energy exchange, drives their function.
main_result: The motor's steady-state dynamics can be characterized by an effective non-Markovian process, yielding four distinct dwell-time distributions observable in single-molecule experiments. The model successfully reproduces known stall forces and mean velocities.
method: The authors employ a theoretical framework using coupled overdamped Brownian motion described by Fokker-Planck equations, simplifying the system via change of variables to analyze relative displacement fluxes.
model_or_system:
The physical system is a dimeric motor moving along filaments. The model incorporates two heads undergoing Brownian motion with periodically switching mobilities governed by a chemical state variable ($
u$), leading to coupled Langevin/Fokker-Planck dynamics.
key_observables: Mean velocity ($V$), energy and information flows, stall force ($f_s$), and the four distinct dwell-time distributions.
important_parameters: Temperature ($k_B T$), mobility switching rates, linker stiffness ($\kappa$), and applied load force ($f$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes overdamped Brownian motion and focuses on localized switching for analytical tractability; the motor is treated as a pure information engine.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates key transport motors (kinesin, myosin) and schematically depicts the mobility-switching model for dimeric heads. Other figures likely detail dynamic distributions or flow calculations.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical system and theoretical model using coupled dynamics; it then analyzes steady-state observables like mean velocity and energy/information flows; finally, it coarse-grains the model to predict measurable quantities like dwell-time distributions.
why_interesting: While focused on classical stochastic processes, the concept of information transduction driving directed motion (Maxwell's demon analogy) connects directly to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and fluctuation theorems relevant in quantum open systems.
